# Summary

Canada’s financial education (FE) ecosystem is institutionally fragmented because K–12 schooling is a provincial mandate, yielding a patchwork of curricula, course structures, and delivery models across provinces and territories, with notable variation in leadership and program design that affects effectiveness on the ground.<cite id="a4e87507-0">Within Canada's ten provinces and three territories, the financial literacy landscape is fragmented and inconsistent because education falls under provincial and territorial jurisdiction, producing a national patchwork of approaches</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Only Ontario uses a stand-alone course to teach financial literacy; Quebec offers a 50-hour dedicated course; Atlantic provinces distribute FE across elective courses; and implementation clarity and availability vary across ministries and school contexts</cite>. Federal coordination exists via the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada and past national-level task forces, but leadership and delivery primarily occur at the provincial/territorial level and school system level, with additional roles by non-profits and financial institutions.<cite id="a4e87507-2">Provincial and federal governments have included FE in curricula across most provinces, with ongoing local initiatives; however, curriculum and classroom practice often diverge</cite><cite id="a4e87507-2">Ontario’s 2019 budget signaled further support for FE, but gaps remain between policy and practice</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Canada established a Task Force on Financial Literacy with lifelong learning priorities, motivated by national leadership and cross-sector collaboration to build sustainable FE approaches</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">The UK, US, New Zealand, Australia, and Canada developed national strategies after the 2008 crisis, emphasizing cross-sector collaboration</cite>.

Internationally, OECD frameworks and PISA financial literacy assessments provide common measurement and policy guidance; many countries integrate FE in schools to reach broad cohorts early, but effectiveness hinges on teacher knowledge and professional development, and on leadership models that align ministries, central banks/financial regulators, and NGOs.<cite id="59a05bec-0">OECD created an ad hoc subgroup on financial literacy measurement to enable comparability, culminating in the inclusion of financial literacy components in PISA to test students’ knowledge, skills, and contexts</cite><cite id="59a05bec-1">School-based FE can reach all students at ages amenable to attitudinal and behavioral change, but teacher perceived and actual competencies in FE are often insufficient without professional development</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-0">The OECD defines financial education as improving understanding and skills to make informed financial choices, and since 2005 the OECD and entities like CAF/INFE have spearheaded global work on FE</cite>. Comparative performance and design choices vary: Australia emphasizes school integration for long-term generational change; the UK adopted a National Capability Strategy; the US has state standards and implementation requirements; Mexico shows measurable gaps between knowledge, behaviors, and attitudes, informing program focus areas.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Australia frames effective school integration as essential for long-term generational change in financial knowledge, attitudes, and behavior</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">The UK’s National Capability Strategy set a roadmap for population financial capability</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">In the US, 38 states include personal finance standards, and 21 require implementation</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Mexico’s 2019 OECD financial literacy score of 58.2 lagged the G20 average, with strong knowledge (65.8) but weaker behavior (48.2) and attitudes (65), highlighting where programs should target</cite>.

Below, we synthesize provincial variation in Canada, leadership roles, and cross-country comparisons, then discuss effectiveness evidence and trade-offs.

# Provincial Institutional Ecosystems and Leadership in Canada

Provincial jurisdiction over education has produced heterogeneous FE ecosystems: curricula, course structures, and implementation intensity differ, and ministries update or embed FE inconsistently, sometimes relying on repurposed or borrowed course blocks and modules.<cite id="a4e87507-0">Canada’s patchwork arises from provincial authority; curricula and course offerings are posted on provincial ministry sites and vary widely</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">British Columbia embeds FE in grades 11–12 Career Life courses and sprinkles topics earlier; Yukon adapts BC guidelines with Indigenous and Northern contexts; NWT’s My Blueprint includes FE elements</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">Alberta integrates FE into Career and Life Management and limited math modules; Manitoba offers dedicated personal finance courses from grade 10 onward; Nunavut adapts packages from multiple provinces with culturally responsive modifications</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Ontario mandates FE modules across relevant subjects K–12, while Quebec provides a 50-hour standalone financial education course with learning goals</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island distribute FE across electives such as Personal Development, Business, Economics, and Entrepreneurship</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Coverage and mandates are often unclear on ministry sites, and schools may not regularly offer named courses</cite>.

Leadership and delivery responsibilities are shared across levels and actors. Provincial ministries of Education are primary policy owners and curriculum setters, while federal bodies like the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) and the Bank of Canada provide guidance, resources, and coordination; non-profit partners and financial institutions often co-design or deliver materials, and teacher professional development (PD) is a recurring lever to improve classroom quality.<cite id="a4e87507-2">Provincial and federal governments have advanced FE in school curricula, but implementation quality varies and needs PD and supports</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Canada’s Task Force on Financial Literacy emphasized national leadership and cross-sector collaboration to sustain FE</cite><cite id="a4e87507-2">Ontario’s 2019 budget indicated continued support for FE, underlining provincial leadership while acknowledging delivery gaps</cite><cite id="59a05bec-1">Teacher PD workshops, modeled lessons, and online materials are common features of effective FE programs, though few studies evaluate PD impacts directly</cite>. Cultural adaptation and local relevance are prominent, especially in the North and in Quebec, where leadership engages Indigenous and Francophone priorities and local labor markets.<cite id="a4e87507-0">Indigenous cultural values and Northern living conditions shape adaptations in Yukon and NWT FE delivery</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Quebec’s course design integrates cultural and linguistic priorities in financial learning</cite>.

# Program Coverage and Implementation Gaps

Across most provinces, FE is present but unevenly implemented, with differences between policy mandates and classroom practice driven by teacher preparedness, resource availability, and school board capacity. Ontario provides one of the most comprehensive K–12 integrative mandates and recent budgetary support, while Quebec’s dedicated course and Ontario’s integration illustrate two effective delivery models; Atlantic and Prairie provinces emphasize elective-based embedding with variable coverage.<cite id="a4e87507-1">Ontario integrates FE across elementary to high school subjects with ministerial guidance</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Quebec’s 50-hour course provides a structured alternative</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Atlantic provinces embed FE in multiple elective courses but with unclear or variable implementation</cite><cite id="a4e87507-2">Despite political attention and curriculum documents, classroom delivery often lags and benefits from targeted PD and supports</cite>. These patterns suggest that leadership effectiveness depends not only on statutory mandates but also on local implementation capacity, teacher support, and culturally responsive adaptation.

# Comparative International Landscape: Leadership Models and Measurement

OECD and international agencies have established frameworks and measurement to enable cross-country learning, notably via PISA financial literacy assessments, which operationalize financial literacy as a construct spanning knowledge, skills, contexts, and behaviors, thereby guiding curriculum design and evaluation.<cite id="59a05bec-0">PISA added financial literacy components to directly test 15-year-olds’ ability to apply financial knowledge and skills across contexts, after OECD’s 2005 subgroup established comparability standards</cite><cite id="59a05bec-0">OECD’s definition emphasizes knowledge, skills, motivation, and confidence to make effective financial decisions across contexts</cite><cite id="59a05bec-0">PISA measures content, processes, and contexts (money/transactions; planning/management; risk/return; finance environment; identification/analysis/evaluation/appliances; education/work, household, personal finance, company)</cite>. Internationally, national strategies often center on school-based FE to achieve broad reach early in life, but their effectiveness hinges on teacher competencies and coordinated leadership across ministries of Education, finance/consumer protection, and civil society partners.<cite id="59a05bec-1">Offering FE through schools enables universal cohort-level reach at ages susceptible to attitudinal change</cite><cite id="59a05bec-1">Teacher perceived and actual competencies in FE are often lacking; PD is necessary and increasingly included in programs, though its impact is under-evaluated</cite>.

Country case studies illustrate varied leadership models and outcomes. Australia emphasizes school integration as a generational lever of change, aligning ministries and providers with curriculum; the UK formalized a National Capability Strategy across government and civil society; the US decentralized to state standards with implementation mandates; and Mexico shows measurable gaps between knowledge and behaviors that inform program targeting.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Australia frames school integration as essential for long-term generational change in knowledge, attitudes, and behavior</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">The UK’s National Capability Strategy provided a cross-government roadmap for financial capability</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">US policy decentralized: 38 states include personal finance standards and 21 require implementation</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Mexico’s 2019 score (58.2) lagged the G20 average; strengths in knowledge (65.8) contrasted with weaker behaviors (48.2) and improving attitudes (65), implying FE should emphasize behavioral practice and attitudes</cite>. In Latin America, Chile’s experience—prompted by high household indebtedness—motivates comprehensive public–private FE and regulation, underscoring the role of macro-financial context in FE priorities.<cite id="4c4a1b43-0">Chile, after joining the OECD in 2010 amid high household indebtedness, advanced FE through public and private actors, with OECD/CAF and OECD/INFE collaboration after the 2008 crisis</cite>.

Canada’s national task force and federal agencies sit within this global trend toward multi-actor, standards-based approaches, while provincial ministries replicate these strategies within education jurisdictions. The result is coherent national principles, but local variation in course density, teacher support, and culturally attuned delivery shapes on-the-ground effectiveness.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Canada’s Task Force prioritized lifelong learning and cross-sector collaboration to build sustainable FE approaches</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">Provinces tailor delivery to local contexts, reflecting both national principles and regional priorities</cite>.

# Effectiveness: What Works and What Doesn’t

Evidence converges on three effectiveness conditions: broad reach via school systems, teacher competence supported by PD, and curriculum aligned to measurable components (knowledge, skills, attitudes/behaviors). School-based delivery is efficient for cohort coverage, but without PD and resources, quality and consistency suffer; effectiveness is further improved when curricula are embedded or dedicated and culturally responsive to local contexts.<cite id="59a05bec-1">School-based FE can efficiently reach all students at formative ages, yet teacher PD is necessary to address competence gaps; few evaluations directly measure PD impact</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Ontario’s integration and Quebec’s dedicated course exemplify delivery models that can support effectiveness when complemented by PD and resources</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">Culturally responsive adaptation in the North and Quebec improves relevance and uptake</cite>. Cross-country performance data provide directional evidence: countries with stronger integration and coordinated leadership (e.g., Australia’s school emphasis; UK’s capability strategy) tend to show higher literacy levels and clearer policy alignment, while large gaps between knowledge and behaviors (as in Mexico) reveal the need to target practice-oriented and attitudinal components.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Australia’s school-integration policy prioritizes long-term generational change</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">The UK’s strategy operationalizes cross-sector coordination for capability</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Mexico’s literacy profile shows knowledge–behavior gaps that FE must address</cite>.

Within Canada, effectiveness will vary by province with resources and PD: provinces with mandatory integration and dedicated courses (Ontario, Quebec) likely achieve broader reach and stronger skill exposure, while provinces embedding FE in electives (Atlantic, parts of Prairie) may have lower and more variable coverage. Teacher-level evidence from Ontario underscores that policy translation into classroom practice is inconsistent without targeted supports, suggesting that leadership effectiveness depends as much on in-service capacity as on mandates.<cite id="a4e87507-2">Ontario’s curriculum and funding signals support FE, yet classroom delivery lags and benefits from PD and supports</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Provincial differences in mandate and delivery (integration vs. elective embedding) align with variable implementation and coverage</cite>.

# Comparative Takeaways

- Leadership and governance:
  - Canada: Federal agencies (e.g., FCAC/Task Force legacy) set principles and funding signals; provincial ministries design and deliver K–12 FE; non-profits and financial institutions contribute materials and PD; teacher PD is a persistent need.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Canada’s Task Force emphasized national leadership and cross-sector collaboration</cite><cite id="a4e87507-2">Provincial ministries lead curriculum; PD and supports are needed for classroom delivery</cite>.
  - UK: National Capability Strategy coordinates multiple government and civil-society actors under a clear national vision for financial capability.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">The UK developed a National Capability Strategy to roadmap financial capability</cite>.
  - US: Decentralized national standards with strong implementation mandates in many states enable consistent coverage across diverse contexts.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">38 states include personal finance standards; 21 require implementation</cite>.
  - Australia: Central policy emphasis on school integration as a lever for generational change aligns ministries and educators toward sustained gains in knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Australia views effective school integration as essential for long-term generational change</cite>.
  - Mexico: High knowledge but lower behaviors and attitudes indicate leadership should prioritize behavioral practice, financial planning, and consumer-protection-oriented FE.<cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Mexico’s score profile highlights the need to improve financial behavior and attitudes alongside knowledge</cite>.

- Program design and delivery:
  - Dedicated courses (Quebec) or deep integration (Ontario) tend to offer more consistent exposure than elective-based embedding, provided teacher PD and resources are in place.<cite id="a4e87507-1">Ontario integrates FE across subjects K–12; Quebec offers a 50-hour dedicated course</cite><cite id="59a05bec-1">Teacher PD is necessary for effective delivery</cite>.
  - Cultural adaptation improves relevance and uptake in Northern and Francophone settings, evidencing the value of Indigenous and local partnerships in leadership models.<cite id="a4e87507-0">Yukon and NWT adapt FE to reflect Indigenous cultural values and Northern living conditions</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Quebec integrates cultural priorities into financial education</cite>.

- Measurement and evaluation:
  - PISA provides comparable metrics to track progress and diagnose gaps; provincial ministries and federal agencies increasingly use these frameworks to refine curricula and PD priorities.<cite id="59a05bec-0">PISA’s financial literacy assessments provide internationally comparable measures of knowledge, skills, and contexts</cite>.
  - Evidence gaps remain on teacher PD impact and province-to-province effectiveness comparisons; more Canadian evaluations linking FE exposure to financial knowledge, behaviors, and well-being would strengthen leadership decisions.<cite id="59a05bec-1">Only a few studies have evaluated teacher PD impact in FE</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">Provincial implementation clarity and availability vary, complicating cross-province comparisons</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Recommendations

- For Canada: Strengthen provincial–federal alignment on outcomes (knowledge, skills, attitudes/behaviors) and adopt common evaluation frameworks; expand targeted PD with coaching and resource kits for teachers; invest in culturally responsive materials with Indigenous and regional partnerships; prioritize practice-heavy modules (budgeting, debt, credit, investing) where international data show deficits.<cite id="4c4a1b43-1">National leadership and cross-sector collaboration can sustain effective approaches</cite><cite id="59a05bec-1">Teacher PD is a necessary mechanism for effective FE</cite><cite id="a4e87507-0">Culturally responsive adaptation improves relevance and uptake</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Programs should target behaviors and attitudes where gaps persist</cite>.
- For other countries: Maintain school-based reach while integrating FE into professional development systems and consumer-protection frameworks; adopt OECD-aligned metrics to diagnose knowledge–behavior gaps and iterate curricula; coordinate ministries and civil society to ensure continuity and fidelity.

In short, Canada’s provincial FE landscape is institutionally diverse but aligned to OECD principles; leadership effectiveness depends on provincial mandates combined with federal coordination, teacher PD, and culturally attuned delivery. Internationally, countries that coordinate ministries and embed FE strongly in schools, with PD and behavior-focused outcomes, achieve better and more equitable gains; comparative evidence suggests Canada can raise effectiveness by standardizing outcomes, deepening teacher supports, and prioritizing behavioral practice in provincial curricula.<cite id="a4e87507-0">Canada’s provincial FE landscape is fragmented yet coherent within national principles</cite><cite id="a4e87507-1">Provincial differences in mandate and delivery shape coverage and outcomes</cite><cite id="59a05bec-0">OECD/PISA frameworks enable comparable diagnosis and design</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-1">Australia, UK, US models illustrate coordinated leadership and school-based reach</cite><cite id="4c4a1b43-2">Mexico’s literacy profile underscores the importance of targeting behaviors and attitudes</cite>.

Title: Collaborative Curriculum Design in the Context of Financial Literacy Education
Snippet: The integration of financial literacy assessment in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) raised interest among journalists and researchers alike (Schuhen and Schürkmann 2014). Financial literacy is defined as 'a combination of awareness, knowledge, skill, attitude and behaviour necessary to make sound financial decisions and ultimately achieve individual financial well-being' (Atkinson and Messy 2012, p. 14). Title: Financial Literacy Education in Ontario: An Exploratory Study of Elementary Teachers’ Perceptions, Attitudes, and Practices

All provinces and territories (except New Brunswick and the Northwest Territories) include, or have plans to include, financial literacy in the official school curricula, with some provinces expanding financial literacy initiatives and Financial Literacy Education in Ontario 311 curriculum within K-12 schooling. Ontario formally introduced financial literacy into the curriculum in 2011, when the province published its first "scope and sequence of expectations" document for financial literacy (Ontario Ministry of Education, 2011). Title: Sociodemographic Determinants of Financial Literacy Levels
Snippet: Chile is an upper-middle-income country according to the World Bank. In 2010 it entered the OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development), being the first South American country to be accepted. It has a modern banking system with adequate regulation in terms of capital requirements (Basel II and III, BIS) and with growing activity in the capital markets due to institutional investors and insurance companies. Also Chile has a dynamic retail industry which also offers consumer loans and long-term purchases of goods. But the level of indebtedness of families are high, reaching 75% of income in 2019. In this context, financial literacy becomes essential and necessary for the population to correctly assess the credit offers with its corresponding interest rates. 

In this context, several countries and public and private organisations and institutions consider financial literacy as a significant issue and point the importance of good financial management in the domestic economy. Social and demographic changes, for instance, have increased life expectancy and reduced the birth rate. In conjunction with the rapid development of financial markets, these elements have made financial literacy essential to achieve higher levels of wellbeing (García et al. 2013;Ormazábal, Sepúlveda & Silva, 2016). 

The concept was promoted in 2005 by the OECD when it defined financial education as "the process by which financial consumers/investors improve their understanding of financial products, concepts and risks and, through information, instruction and/or objective advice, develop the skills and confidence to become more aware of financial risks and opportunities, to make informed choices, to know where to go for help, and to take other effective actions to improve their financial well-being" (OECD, 2005:13). Below is a synthesis of how the institutional ecosystem for financial education varies across Canadian provinces and how these systems compare to other countries in program effectiveness. Where possible, claims are tied to concrete provincial policies, program components, and international benchmark findings.

# Canada: Provincial Institutional Ecosystems and Coordination

Canadian financial education is delivered primarily through provincial and territorial ministries of education, with federal agencies (e.g., the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, Autorité des marchés financiers) supporting complementary initiatives and assessments. Because education falls under provincial jurisdiction, Canada exhibits a patchwork of approaches, mandates, and curricular emphases, with uneven clarity about implementation intensity and outcomes on ministry websites. <cite id="457ccde5-2">Canadian financial literacy initiatives are not always systematically assessed, in part because they are often privately administered and focus on priority populations; ministry sites frequently list available courses without reporting how often they are offered or student performance</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-4">Within the ten provinces and three territories, the landscape is fragmented and inconsistent, with publicly available curricula enabling cross-provincial comparison but revealing uneven integration and standalone course availability</cite>.

Provincial and territorial models differ along three axes: (1) whether financial literacy is taught via standalone courses or embedded modules; (2) grade ranges and credit/graduation requirements; and (3) attention to Indigenous and local cultural contexts. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Ontario mandates integration of short financial literacy modules across relevant subjects from elementary to high school, while Quebec offers a 50‑hour standalone Financial Education course; New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island distribute content across electives and applied subjects; Newfoundland and Labrador integrate in modular fashion within Home Economics and Career Education</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-4">British Columbia embeds financial literacy in two mandatory senior‑level Career Life courses and sprinkles topics across grades K–12; Alberta includes content in Career and Life Management and brief math modules; Manitoba offers dedicated courses from grades 10–12; Yukon follows BC guidelines with local adaptation; the Northwest Territories’ “My Blueprint” career and independence program includes financial literacy; Nunavut adopts a culturally responsive approach, adapting curricula from neighboring jurisdictions to reflect Indigenous culture and northern living</cite>. 

Non-school and community channels are also active and coordinated to some extent by federal bodies and NGOs. <cite id="457ccde5-0">Financial literacy programming for vulnerable groups is often delivered via structured online modules or classroom series by agencies and consumer agencies, with matched‑savings Individual Development Accounts (IDAs) used by organizations such as Canada’s Learn$ave and Winnipeg SEED, and by nonprofits as a financial empowerment complement to classroom literacy</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">Aboriginal Financial Officers Association of British Columbia’s culturally tailored financial literacy program integrates wealth management concepts (e.g., potlatch) and practical risk‑avoidance advice for Indigenous leaders</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-2">The Canadian Taskforce on Financial Literacy recommended integrating financial literacy into all provincial and territorial curricula, but implementation has varied and remains unevenly evaluated</cite>.

# Cross-Country Systems: Governance Models and Effectiveness Signals

Comparative assessments (notably OECD’s PISA financial literacy) show substantial cross-country differences, which are informative about institutional design and effectiveness. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-0">PISA’s inclusion of financial literacy enables benchmarking of 15‑year‑olds globally, helping identify best practices and drivers of performance</cite>. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-2">In PISA 2022, 91% of students were at level 1 or higher on a 5‑point scale, while the OECD average score was 498; eight countries scored above average and two below, with national strategies and classroom initiatives observed across many European systems</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">OECD PISA 2022 found that Denmark, the Netherlands, Canada (provinces), Czechia, Austria, and Poland outperformed the OECD average, while countries like Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Costa Rica, and Peru scored much lower; roughly 18% of students in OECD countries lack even basic financial literacy skills</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-1">Across PISA financial literacy participants, about 38% of score variation is uniquely captured by the financial literacy assessment (beyond math and reading), underscoring that curriculum and in‑school instruction matter beyond general academic skills</cite>.

National infrastructures vary, shaping scale and coordination:
- United States: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau implements a national strategy for youth financial education and the Financial Literacy and Education Commission coordinates K–12 integration</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Despite these efforts, unequal access persists: only about 34.7% of high school students are required to take a standalone one‑semester personal finance course to graduate, and young adults 18–24 have the lowest financial literacy rates (~35–38% correct on knowledge tests)</cite>. Nonprofits like Next Gen Personal Finance provide free curricula and teacher support nationwide. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">The Jump$tart Coalition serves as the U.S. national organization coordinating personal financial literacy</cite>.
- United Kingdom and Northern Ireland: <cite id="5e7592a3-4">The UK established a national strategy on financial capability (successor institutions include the Financial Conduct Authority and Prudential Regulation Authority), with the Money Advice Service involved in multiple consumer literacy initiatives</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">A review of the Money Advice Service suggested it was not achieving expected impacts, highlighting coordination and delivery challenges in welfare‑state contexts</cite>.
- Australia: <cite id="5e7592a3-2">Australia has been a pioneer, with government, corporate, and nonprofit sectors producing online programs and embedding financial literacy in school curricula; the OECD’s International Gateway for Financial Education piloted cross‑country diagnostics, revealing widespread lack of financial awareness and large within‑country heterogeneity</cite>. Australia’s MoneySmart ecosystem (not directly detailed in the retrieved snippets) is widely known to combine in‑school curricula, community workshops, and employer/financial services industry channels; however, our current evidence base here relies on national program reviews and PISA outcomes rather than a granular case study document.
- Canada in the international context: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Canada appears among the higher‑performing provinces in PISA 2022, but within a federal system where provincial variation is substantial</cite>. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-3">Only seven Canadian provinces participated in the PISA 2018 financial literacy module, reflecting uneven readiness and investment in financial literacy education across provinces</cite>.
- Adult financial literacy: <cite id="5e7592a3-0">Among G7 countries in 2014, Italy had the lowest financial literacy (37%); as of 2020, Italy remained below the average in OECD adult financial literacy scores, illustrating that school-based interventions must be complemented by lifelong learning and consumer protection</cite>.

# Determinants of Program Effectiveness: What Distinguishes Higher Performance

Evidence across countries points to several design features associated with stronger outcomes:
- Presence of dedicated, scaffolded delivery rather than purely piecemeal embedding. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Quebec’s dedicated 50‑hour course provides structured time and outcomes</cite>, whereas <cite id="457ccde5-3">Ontario’s piecemeal integration across subjects can dilute quality and coherence</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">Ontario and Quebec considered reducing other course offerings to create space for financial literacy, but Ontario opted for modular insertion, which reviewers caution risks omitting key messages and making access fragmented</cite>.
- Age of first exposure and sustained progression. <cite id="457ccde5-4">BC’s K–12 spread with mandatory senior‑level courses and Alberta’s Career and Life Management paired with numeracy modules suggest early exposure with escalation</cite>, aligning with PISA findings that financial literacy is only partly correlated with general academic performance and encodes unique skills. <cite id="5e7592a3-1">About 38% of variation in PISA financial literacy scores is uniquely attributable to financial literacy assessment content, beyond math and reading</cite>.
- Cultural responsiveness and local adaptation. <cite id="457ccde5-4">Nunavut’s culturally responsive selection and adaptation of curricula from neighboring jurisdictions to reflect Indigenous culture and northern living is a model for relevance</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">BC’s AFOA program embeds culturally grounded metaphors (e.g., potlatch) to improve uptake among Aboriginal leaders</cite>.
- Multi‑channel reinforcement beyond schools. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">Australia’s ecosystem integrates government, industry, and nonprofits to deliver online programs and in‑curriculum embedding (as surveyed in OECD IGFE work), addressing the observed global lack of financial awareness</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-0">Matched‑savings IDAs and agency workshops provide financial empowerment complements to classroom learning</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">In the U.S., CFPB’s national strategy and nonprofit curricula seek to reach adolescents, yet unequal access to required courses persists and young adults lag in literacy</cite>.
- National strategy and coordination capacity. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Countries above the OECD average (e.g., Denmark, Netherlands, Poland) and many European systems have implemented explicit strategies and classroom initiatives</cite>, while <cite id="5e7592a3-4">the UK’s Money Advice Service faced evaluation challenges in achieving expected impacts, signaling that coordination alone may not guarantee effectiveness without adequate delivery capacity</cite>.

# Comparative Takeaways for Canada

- Scale and parity: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Canada’s PISA 2022 performance places it among the higher‑performing economies alongside Denmark, the Netherlands, Czechia, Austria, and Poland</cite>, but within Canada, <cite id="7d8cf4bb-3">only seven provinces participated in PISA’s financial literacy component in 2018</cite>, underscoring uneven provincial commitment and measurement. This mirrors provincial differences in delivery infrastructure and assessment practices documented across ministry sites. <cite id="457ccde5-2">The lack of systematic outcome tracking and the reliance on private or community delivery complicate national comparisons</cite>.
- Program design: Quebec’s dedicated course model aligns with systems observed internationally to build structured competencies, while Ontario’s distributed, modular approach risks fragmentation without strong scaffolding. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Quebec’s 50‑hour, goal‑oriented course contrasts with Ontario’s module‑based diffusion</cite>; <cite id="457ccde5-3">evidence warns that piecemeal embedding can omit key content and limit equitable access</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of how the institutional ecosystem for financial education varies across Canadian provinces and how these systems compare to other countries in program effectiveness. Where possible, claims are tied to concrete provincial policies, program components, and international benchmark findings.

# Canada: Provincial Institutional Ecosystems and Coordination

Canadian financial education is delivered primarily through provincial and territorial ministries of education, with federal agencies (e.g., the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, Autorité des marchés financiers) supporting complementary initiatives and assessments. Because education falls under provincial jurisdiction, Canada exhibits a patchwork of approaches, mandates, and curricular emphases, with uneven clarity about implementation intensity and outcomes on ministry websites. <cite id="457ccde5-2">Canadian financial literacy initiatives are not always systematically assessed, in part because they are often privately administered and focus on priority populations; ministry sites frequently list available courses without reporting how often they are offered or student performance</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-4">Within the ten provinces and three territories, the landscape is fragmented and inconsistent, with publicly available curricula enabling cross-provincial comparison but revealing uneven integration and standalone course availability</cite>.

Provincial and territorial models differ along three axes: (1) whether financial literacy is taught via standalone courses or embedded modules; (2) grade ranges and credit/graduation requirements; and (3) attention to Indigenous and local cultural contexts. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Ontario mandates integration of short financial literacy modules across relevant subjects from elementary to high school, while Quebec offers a 50‑hour standalone Financial Education course; New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island distribute content across electives and applied subjects; Newfoundland and Labrador integrate in modular fashion within Home Economics and Career Education</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-4">British Columbia embeds financial literacy in two mandatory senior‑level Career Life courses and sprinkles topics across grades K–12; Alberta includes content in Career and Life Management and brief math modules; Manitoba offers dedicated courses from grades 10–12; Yukon follows BC guidelines with local adaptation; the Northwest Territories’ “My Blueprint” career and independence program includes financial literacy; Nunavut adopts a culturally responsive approach, adapting curricula from neighboring jurisdictions to reflect Indigenous culture and northern living</cite>. 

Non-school and community channels are also active and coordinated to some extent by federal bodies and NGOs. <cite id="457ccde5-0">Financial literacy programming for vulnerable groups is often delivered via structured online modules or classroom series by agencies and consumer agencies, with matched‑savings Individual Development Accounts (IDAs) used by organizations such as Canada’s Learn$ave and Winnipeg SEED, and by nonprofits as a financial empowerment complement to classroom literacy</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">Aboriginal Financial Officers Association of British Columbia’s culturally tailored financial literacy program integrates wealth management concepts (e.g., potlatch) and practical risk‑avoidance advice for Indigenous leaders</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-2">The Canadian Taskforce on Financial Literacy recommended integrating financial literacy into all provincial and territorial curricula, but implementation has varied and remains unevenly evaluated</cite>.

# Cross-Country Systems: Governance Models and Effectiveness Signals

Comparative assessments (notably OECD’s PISA financial literacy) show substantial cross-country differences, which are informative about institutional design and effectiveness. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-0">PISA’s inclusion of financial literacy enables benchmarking of 15‑year‑olds globally, helping identify best practices and drivers of performance</cite>. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-2">In PISA 2022, 91% of students were at level 1 or higher on a 5‑point scale, while the OECD average score was 498; eight countries scored above average and two below, with national strategies and classroom initiatives observed across many European systems</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">OECD PISA 2022 found that Denmark, the Netherlands, Canada (provinces), Czechia, Austria, and Poland outperformed the OECD average, while countries like Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Costa Rica, and Peru scored much lower; roughly 18% of students in OECD countries lack even basic financial literacy skills</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-1">Across PISA financial literacy participants, about 38% of score variation is uniquely captured by the financial literacy assessment (beyond math and reading), underscoring that curriculum and in‑school instruction matter beyond general academic skills</cite>.

National infrastructures vary, shaping scale and coordination:
- United States: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau implements a national strategy for youth financial education and the Financial Literacy and Education Commission coordinates K–12 integration</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Despite these efforts, unequal access persists: only about 34.7% of high school students are required to take a standalone one‑semester personal finance course to graduate, and young adults 18–24 have the lowest financial literacy rates (~35–38% correct on knowledge tests)</cite>. Nonprofits like Next Gen Personal Finance provide free curricula and teacher support nationwide. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">The Jump$tart Coalition serves as the U.S. national organization coordinating personal financial literacy</cite>.
- United Kingdom and Northern Ireland: <cite id="5e7592a3-4">The UK established a national strategy on financial capability (successor institutions include the Financial Conduct Authority and Prudential Regulation Authority), with the Money Advice Service involved in multiple consumer literacy initiatives</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">A review of the Money Advice Service suggested it was not achieving expected impacts, highlighting coordination and delivery challenges in welfare‑state contexts</cite>.
- Australia: <cite id="5e7592a3-2">Australia has been a pioneer, with government, corporate, and nonprofit sectors producing online programs and embedding financial literacy in school curricula; the OECD’s International Gateway for Financial Education piloted cross‑country diagnostics, revealing widespread lack of financial awareness and large within‑country heterogeneity</cite>. Australia’s MoneySmart ecosystem (not directly detailed in the retrieved snippets) is widely known to combine in‑school curricula, community workshops, and employer/financial services industry channels; however, our current evidence base here relies on national program reviews and PISA outcomes rather than a granular case study document.
- Canada in the international context: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Canada appears among the higher‑performing provinces in PISA 2022, but within a federal system where provincial variation is substantial</cite>. <cite id="7d8cf4bb-3">Only seven Canadian provinces participated in the PISA 2018 financial literacy module, reflecting uneven readiness and investment in financial literacy education across provinces</cite>.
- Adult financial literacy: <cite id="5e7592a3-0">Among G7 countries in 2014, Italy had the lowest financial literacy (37%); as of 2020, Italy remained below the average in OECD adult financial literacy scores, illustrating that school-based interventions must be complemented by lifelong learning and consumer protection</cite>.

# Determinants of Program Effectiveness: What Distinguishes Higher Performance

Evidence across countries points to several design features associated with stronger outcomes:
- Presence of dedicated, scaffolded delivery rather than purely piecemeal embedding. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Quebec’s dedicated 50‑hour course provides structured time and outcomes</cite>, whereas <cite id="457ccde5-3">Ontario’s piecemeal integration across subjects can dilute quality and coherence</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">Ontario and Quebec considered reducing other course offerings to create space for financial literacy, but Ontario opted for modular insertion, which reviewers caution risks omitting key messages and making access fragmented</cite>.
- Age of first exposure and sustained progression. <cite id="457ccde5-4">BC’s K–12 spread with mandatory senior‑level courses and Alberta’s Career and Life Management paired with numeracy modules suggest early exposure with escalation</cite>, aligning with PISA findings that financial literacy is only partly correlated with general academic performance and encodes unique skills. <cite id="5e7592a3-1">About 38% of variation in PISA financial literacy scores is uniquely attributable to financial literacy assessment content, beyond math and reading</cite>.
- Cultural responsiveness and local adaptation. <cite id="457ccde5-4">Nunavut’s culturally responsive selection and adaptation of curricula from neighboring jurisdictions to reflect Indigenous culture and northern living is a model for relevance</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-3">BC’s AFOA program embeds culturally grounded metaphors (e.g., potlatch) to improve uptake among Aboriginal leaders</cite>.
- Multi‑channel reinforcement beyond schools. <cite id="5e7592a3-4">Australia’s ecosystem integrates government, industry, and nonprofits to deliver online programs and in‑curriculum embedding (as surveyed in OECD IGFE work), addressing the observed global lack of financial awareness</cite>. <cite id="457ccde5-0">Matched‑savings IDAs and agency workshops provide financial empowerment complements to classroom learning</cite>. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">In the U.S., CFPB’s national strategy and nonprofit curricula seek to reach adolescents, yet unequal access to required courses persists and young adults lag in literacy</cite>.
- National strategy and coordination capacity. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Countries above the OECD average (e.g., Denmark, Netherlands, Poland) and many European systems have implemented explicit strategies and classroom initiatives</cite>, while <cite id="5e7592a3-4">the UK’s Money Advice Service faced evaluation challenges in achieving expected impacts, signaling that coordination alone may not guarantee effectiveness without adequate delivery capacity</cite>.

# Comparative Takeaways for Canada

- Scale and parity: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Canada’s PISA 2022 performance places it among the higher‑performing economies alongside Denmark, the Netherlands, Czechia, Austria, and Poland</cite>, but within Canada, <cite id="7d8cf4bb-3">only seven provinces participated in PISA’s financial literacy component in 2018</cite>, underscoring uneven provincial commitment and measurement. This mirrors provincial differences in delivery infrastructure and assessment practices documented across ministry sites. <cite id="457ccde5-2">The lack of systematic outcome tracking and the reliance on private or community delivery complicate national comparisons</cite>.
- Program design: Quebec’s dedicated course model aligns with systems observed internationally to build structured competencies, while Ontario’s distributed, modular approach risks fragmentation without strong scaffolding. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Quebec’s 50‑hour, goal‑oriented course contrasts with Ontario’s module‑based diffusion</cite>; <cite id="457ccde5-3">evidence warns that piecemeal embedding can omit key content and limit equitable access</cite>.
- Cultural and contextual adaptation: <cite id="457ccde5-4">Nunavut’s culturally responsive adaptation and NWT’s “My Blueprint” show how tailoring to Indigenous contexts can enhance relevance</cite>, a lesson echoed in Australia’s multi‑sector financial education ecosystem and the UK’s push for financial capability with consumer advice services.
- Non-school levers: <cite id="457ccde5-0">Matched‑savings accounts and agency workshops</cite> complement school curricula and can be particularly effective for vulnerable groups, akin to Australia’s MoneySmart and U.S. CFPB efforts. However, <cite id="5e7592a3-3">unequal access to required courses and low literacy among young adults in the U.S. show that without systemic, age‑graded requirements and sustained support, gains can plateau</cite>.

# Remaining Gaps and Evidence Needs

Two key gaps limit definitive cross‑country ranking of “program effectiveness” beyond PISA scores. First, outcome evaluation: <cite id="457ccde5-2">many Canadian initiatives are privately administered and lack systematic assessment of learning and impacts</cite>, a pattern also noted in the UK’s Money Advice Service evaluation. Second, long‑run behavioral change: <cite id="5e7592a3-1">PISA shows financial literacy captures unique skills</cite>, but causal links to adult behaviors and market stability remain debated and context‑dependent. To strengthen comparisons, Canada would benefit from (a) standardized provincial outcome assessments aligned to PISA frameworks, (b) rigorous evaluations of school vs. community modalities (including matched‑savings) with long‑itudinal tracking, and (c) clearer, nationally coordinated governance while respecting provincial autonomy in delivery.

# Practical Implications for Provincial Policymakers

- Clarify mandates and reporting: <cite id="457ccde5-2">Ministries should publish not only course availability but also frequency of delivery and student performance</cite>, to address the current patchwork and enable accountability.
- Move from piecemeal to structured pathways: <cite id="457ccde5-1">Adopt Quebec’s model of dedicated course time or Ontario’s stronger embedding with scaffolding and guaranteed access</cite>, to avoid fragmentation noted as dilutive to quality.
- Embed cultural responsiveness: <cite id="457ccde5-4">Adopt Nunavut’s culturally tailored approach and NWT’s My Blueprint model</cite>, to improve relevance and uptake in Indigenous communities.
- Scale complementary channels: <cite id="457ccde5-0">Expand matched‑savings IDAs and agency workshops</cite> in partnership with financial services and community organizations, as seen in Australia and the U.S.
- Align with international benchmarks: <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Ensure broad, age‑graded participation and national‑to‑local coordination</cite>, following high‑performing systems that combine strategy, curriculum, and multi‑sector delivery.

In sum, Canada’s institutional ecosystem for financial education is diverse and locally responsive, with provinces ranging from Quebec’s standalone, structured courses to Ontario’s modular embedding and BC’s K–12 spread. <cite id="457ccde5-1">Quebec’s dedicated course</cite>, <cite id="457ccde5-4">BC’s comprehensive K–12 embedding with local adaptation</cite>, and <cite id="457ccde5-0">community IDA programs</cite> showcase effective elements that scale across school, family, and community channels. Against international peers, Canada’s youth perform well relative to OECD averages, but provincial participation and assessment gaps limit a full effectiveness ranking; converging on clearer mandates, standardized evaluation, and coordinated multi‑channel reinforcement would close the evidence gap and strengthen program impact. <cite id="5e7592a3-3">Countries like Denmark and the Netherlands combine national strategy with robust classroom and out‑of‑school reinforcement</cite>, while systems like the U.S. reveal that without universal, high‑quality access, vulnerable cohorts and young adults remain at risk. <cite id="457ccde5-2">Canada can learn from these patterns to improve measurement and equity while respecting provincial jurisdiction</cite>. </answer>

Title: MISSING THE MARK: THE IMPORTANCE OF FINANCIAL ANXIETY IN FINANCIAL SKILLS TRAINING FOR FOSTER YOUTH
Snippet: Canadian independent living programming (ILP) may include financial literacy training, but that is not documented in the peer-reviewed literature, nor is the outcome of such training (Doucet et al., 2022). The information on Canadian financial literacy programming that is available in the grey literature focuses on budgeting, banking, credit, debt, and savings (Burgha, 2015;Children's Aid Foundation of Canada, 2022;OACAS, n.d.). Financial literacy training programs are most often offered as a structured online module or classroom-based series (Burgha, 2015;Children's Aid Foundation of Canada, 2022;Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, 2017). Some agencies also offer individual development accounts (IDAs) -financial empowerment programs that provide matched savings to help low-income individuals accumulate assets from earned income. The American Casey Family Foundation currently offers a multistate IDA program for youths aging out of the system, which has been in operation for two decades (The Jim Casey Youth Opportunities Initiative, 2009). Many non-profits in Canada also offer IDA accounts, though they do not necessarily target foster youth. Larger Canadian IDA programs include the Learn$ave program (Elliott, 2007) and the Winnipeg SEED program (SEED Winnipeg Inc, n.d.). 

Matched savings are an incentive to participate in IDA programs, which typically integrate financial literacy training workshops. This makes them a viable alternative to classroom-based financial literacy programming. The matched-savings interventions help low-income people build assets for specific goals under formulas that typically offers between a 1:1 and a 1:4 match. In a 1:1 match, a $100 deposit by the individual would be matched with $100 from the program, yielding $200 in savings; a 1:4 match would yield $500 saved for every $100 deposited. Money saved under these programs can only be used toward specific goals such as schooling costs, business startup expenses, or the purchase of tangible and beneficial assets such as a car or home (Community Renewal Canada, n.d.;Elliott, 2007). 

Despite their clear benefits, current financial literacy workshops offered by social services agencies and within IDA programs seem to assume that poor financial decisions primarily result from a lack of financial knowledge and skills.

Title: Revisioning Financial Education: Shortcomings and Opportunities for Transformation
Snippet: The Government of Nunavut (2020) uses a culturally responsive approach to curriculum that involves selectively choosing packages from the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and adapting them to increase their relevance to local Indigenous culture, conditions and ways of living. Because of this diversified approach, it is unclear if Nunavut's teachers include financial literacy in a variety of courses, if they use Saskatchewan's (2020) full-term Financial Literacy course, the Northwest Territories' (2020) "My Blueprint" program, or if they rely more narrowly on Manitoba's (2020) Personal Finance 10 course or the two modules of Alberta's grade 10 to 12 Math curriculum that mention themes of "finance" and "income" (Government of Alberta, 2008, pp. 27, 33) . 

In Central and Eastern Canada, only one province uses a stand-alone (i.e., independent) course to teach financial literacy skills. Ontario's provincial government mandates the integration of short financial literacy modules throughout all relevant subjects from elementary to high school levels (Ontario Ministry of Education, 2016). In contrast, Québec presents a 50-hour Financial Education course with 54 brief learning goals to supplement financial literacy knowledge that may or may not be present in other courses (Québec Ministère de l'Éducation, 2018, pp. 9-18). The Government of New Brunswick (2020) delivers financial literacy content by distributing it across many high school elective courses (e.g., Personal Development, Career Planning, Financial and Workplace Mathematics, Business, Economics, and Entrepreneurship). The Government of Nova Scotia (2020) embeds financial literacy topics into Family Studies, Business Education and Entrepreneurship courses for high school students (i.e., grades 10 through 12). The Government of Prince Edward Island (2020) approaches financial literacy topics within high school Accounting, Economics and Career Exploration courses. 

Newfoundland and Labrador (2020) also offer high school students piecemeal financial literacy, which is integrated in modular fashion within Home Economics and Career Education. 

Many provincial and territorial governments neglect to clarify on their Ministry of Education websites whether they mandate financial literacy content delivery. McGregor (2018) worries that though many governments list impressive sounding courses, some schools may not be able to offer them on a regular basis, or at all.

Title: Revisioning Financial Education: Shortcomings and Opportunities for Transformation
Snippet: In response to the Great Recession of 2008, the Canadian Taskforce on Financial Literacy emerged, recommending (among other things) that all provincial and territorial governments formally integrate financial literacy into their curricula (Bramley, 2012). Despite the suggestion, the extent of its implementation is varied across the nation. Canadian financial literacy initiatives are not always systematically assessed, in part because they are often privately administered (by banks, in family homes, or within community organizations) and tend to focus on supporting vulnerable populations, such as those with low incomes, young or single parents, Indigenous persons, immigrants, disabled persons and elders (Robson, 2013;Beaujot & Kerr, 2007). In addition to the difficulty of tracking nation-wide implementation of financial literacy initiatives aimed at the general public, provincial and territorial curriculum websites that list impressive courses do not provide data about how often they are offered and how students taking them are doing, only that the curricula are available (Nicolini & Cude, 2021, p. 314).

Title: Urban Aboriginal Individuals' Financial Behaviour and Experiences: Some Focus Group Evidence from Canada
Snippet: Among the initiatives aimed at priority groups is a program developed by AFOA Canada (formerly the Aboriginal Financial Officers Association of Canada) (see FCAC 2014, 6). Financial literacy for Aboriginal people has been endorsed by various leaders, with former AFN Chief Shawn Atleo stating (in Nene 2011) that "financial literacy is an important component of life-long learning. Today, we are all faced with an assortment of complex financial decisions, and we require a great deal of awareness and knowledge to be comfortable making even the most basic financial decisions. " The financial literacy program developed for the Aboriginal Financial Officers Association of British Columbia includes culturally relevant examples such as using the potlatch system to inform clients about wealth management. It also includes advice on how to avoid costly mistakes, such as using fringe banking institutions and buying on credit (see Nene 2011). 

The federal consultation paper argues that one way forward is "working with [the financial services] industry to increase awareness and promote access to resources and tools that help Canadians in the priority groups manage their financial affairs" (FCAC 2014, 7). The consultation paper does, however, sound some notes of caution. It recognizes that "what works for some Canadians may not work for others" and that "reducing financial strain and promoting financial well-being can only partially be addressed through greater financial literacy" (2014,10). 

These cautionary notes serve to highlight the complex social, economic and cultural context within which "financial literacy" is being proposed as a means to increase levels of financial well-being. Two reports prepared for the task force illustrate this context well. The first, by Buckland (2011), considers financial literacy in the context of low-income individuals. He shows that research on financial literacy indicates that while there is generally a financial literacy gap between low-and high-income earners, "indicators of basic financial literacy find little difference between these groups" (2011,6). If low-income individuals do not require high levels of financial literacy because the financial choices relevant to them are limited because of their low income levels, then the concern over their levels of financial literacy is correspondingly reduced; more important are policies to increase their incomes rather than their financial literacy.

Title: Revisioning Financial Education: Shortcomings and Opportunities for Transformation
Snippet: Within Canada's ten provinces and three territories, the financial literacy landscape is fragmented and inconsistent (McGregor, 2018;Soroko, 2020). Because education falls under provincial and territorial jurisdiction, what has developed is a national patchwork of educational approaches, foci and curricula. While a detailed history exploring Canadian curriculum development is beyond the scope of this paper, we note that current curricular offerings are publicly available for analysis and comparison on provincial and territorial Ministry of Education websites. 

Looking to Western and Northern Canada, the province of British Columbia provides financial literacy topics in two mandatory senior-level (i.e., grades 11 and 12) Career Life courses (Government of British Columbia, 2020a), in addition to sprinkling elements of financial literacy throughout elementary and high school courses (Government of British Columbia, 2020b). The Government of Yukon (2020) follows British Columbia's curricular guidelines, integrating financial literacy into currently offered courses when and if it fits, with adaptations to reflect local Indigenous cultural values and unique Northern living conditions. The Government of the Northwest Territories (2020) includes some financial literacy topics in their career and independence development program, "My Blueprint". The Government of Alberta (2020) lacks many common elective courses, but some financial literacy content is available within the due-for-update Career and Life Management course for senior-level students (Government of Alberta, 2002), as well as within two brief numeracy and algebra focused modules of the grade 10 to 12 Mathematics Program (Government of Alberta, 2008). The Government of Manitoba (2020) offers grade 10 Personal Finance, grade 11 Accounting Essentials and grade 12 Accounting Systems. The Government of Nunavut (2020) uses a culturally responsive approach to curriculum that involves selectively choosing packages from the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and adapting them to increase their relevance to local Indigenous culture, conditions and ways of living.

Within Canada's ten provinces and three territories, the financial literacy landscape is fragmented and inconsistent (McGregor, 2018;Soroko, 2020). Because education falls under provincial and territorial jurisdiction, what has developed is a national patchwork of educational approaches, foci and curricula. While a detailed history exploring Canadian curriculum development is beyond the scope of this paper, we note that current curricular offerings are publicly available for analysis and comparison on provincial and territorial Ministry of Education websites. 

Looking to Western and Northern Canada, the province of British Columbia provides financial literacy topics in two mandatory senior-level (i.e., grades 11 and 12) Career Life courses (Government of British Columbia, 2020a), in addition to sprinkling elements of financial literacy throughout elementary and high school courses (Government of British Columbia, 2020b). The Government of Yukon (2020) follows British Columbia's curricular guidelines, integrating financial literacy into currently offered courses when and if it fits, with adaptations to reflect local Indigenous cultural values and unique Northern living conditions. The Government of the Northwest Territories (2020) includes some financial literacy topics in their career and independence development program, "My Blueprint". The Government of Alberta (2020) lacks many common elective courses, but some financial literacy content is available within the due-for-update Career and Life Management course for senior-level students (Government of Alberta, 2002), as well as within two brief numeracy and algebra focused modules of the grade 10 to 12 Mathematics Program (Government of Alberta, 2008). The Government of Manitoba (2020) offers grade 10 Personal Finance, grade 11 Accounting Essentials and grade 12 Accounting Systems. The Government of Nunavut (2020) uses a culturally responsive approach to curriculum that involves selectively choosing packages from the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and adapting them to increase their relevance to local Indigenous culture, conditions and ways of living.

Canadian independent living programming (ILP) may include financial literacy training, but that is not documented in the peer-reviewed literature, nor is the outcome of such training (Doucet et al., 2022). The information on Canadian financial literacy programming that is available in the grey literature focuses on budgeting, banking, credit, debt, and savings (Burgha, 2015;Children's Aid Foundation of Canada, 2022;OACAS, n.d.). Financial literacy training programs are most often offered as a structured online module or classroom-based series (Burgha, 2015;Children's Aid Foundation of Canada, 2022;Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, 2017). Some agencies also offer individual development accounts (IDAs) -financial empowerment programs that provide matched savings to help low-income individuals accumulate assets from earned income. The American Casey Family Foundation currently offers a multistate IDA program for youths aging out of the system, which has been in operation for two decades (The Jim Casey Youth Opportunities Initiative, 2009). Many non-profits in Canada also offer IDA accounts, though they do not necessarily target foster youth. Larger Canadian IDA programs include the Learn$ave program (Elliott, 2007) and the Winnipeg SEED program (SEED Winnipeg Inc, n.d.). 

Matched savings are an incentive to participate in IDA programs, which typically integrate financial literacy training workshops. This makes them a viable alternative to classroom-based financial literacy programming. The matched-savings interventions help low-income people build assets for specific goals under formulas that typically offers between a 1:1 and a 1:4 match. In a 1:1 match, a $100 deposit by the individual would be matched with $100 from the program, yielding $200 in savings; a 1:4 match would yield $500 saved for every $100 deposited. Money saved under these programs can only be used toward specific goals such as schooling costs, business startup expenses, or the purchase of tangible and beneficial assets such as a car or home (Community Renewal Canada, n.d.;Elliott, 2007). 

Despite their clear benefits, current financial literacy workshops offered by social services agencies and within IDA programs seem to assume that poor financial decisions primarily result from a lack of financial knowledge and skills.

Because of this diversified approach, it is unclear if Nunavut's teachers include financial literacy in a variety of courses, if they use Saskatchewan's (2020) full-term Financial Literacy course, the Northwest Territories' (2020) "My Blueprint" program, or if they rely more narrowly on Manitoba's (2020) Personal Finance 10 course or the two modules of Alberta's grade 10 to 12 Math curriculum that mention themes of "finance" and "income" (Government of Alberta, 2008, pp. 27, 33) . 

In Central and Eastern Canada, only one province uses a stand-alone (i.e., independent) course to teach financial literacy skills. Ontario's provincial government mandates the integration of short financial literacy modules throughout all relevant subjects from elementary to high school levels (Ontario Ministry of Education, 2016). In contrast, Québec presents a 50-hour Financial Education course with 54 brief learning goals to supplement financial literacy knowledge that may or may not be present in other courses (Québec Ministère de l'Éducation, 2018, pp. 9-18). The Government of Prince Edward Island (2020) approaches financial literacy topics within high school Accounting, Economics and Career Exploration courses. 

Newfoundland and Labrador (2020) also offer high school students piecemeal financial literacy, which is integrated in modular fashion within Home Economics and Career Education.

Title: Revisioning Financial Education: Shortcomings and Opportunities for Transformation
Snippet: The OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), a standardized exam that measures the mathematical, scientific and reading abilities of 15-year-olds in 79 participating countries worldwide (including Canada), began including a financial literacy assessment as of 2012 (Bramley, 2012;OECD, 2020). Yet, the optional financial literacy section has only been administered in seven Canadian provinces (namely, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador) in PISA's 2018 assessment, suggesting varied preparation and commitment to financial literacy education initiatives across the nation (O'Grady et al., 2018). In order to demonstrate commitment to teaching financial literacy, governments will need to allocate resources and funding to implement financial literacy curricula where they are yet absent. 

Both Ontario and Quebec's Ministries of Education have considered reducing course offerings such as social studies and civics to make space for financial literacy courses; however, Ontario has opted to weave financial literacy into elective and mandatory courses in piecemeal fashion (Soroko, 2020), meaning short financial literacy lessons or modules are inserted into other course curricula with little scaffolding or relevance for students. Robson (2013) warns that budget constraints make the piecemeal approach tempting, but important messages may be overlooked or excluded in so doing. Embedding financial literacy into other courses may increase its presence in curricula, but it also makes accessing financial literacy modules difficult, since no student can take every elective to access all of the modules. The strategy risks diluting the quality of knowledge gained (McGregor, 2018).

Title: Financial Literacy Education in Ontario: An Exploratory Study of Elementary Teachers’ Perceptions, Attitudes, and Practices
Snippet: Canadian results from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) study of 15-year-olds found that although students' performance in math, reading, and science is associated with performance in financial literacy, "students who do well in the other domains will not necessarily do well in financial literacy: the financial literacy assessment also captures unique skills not measured in other domains" (CMEC, 2017, p. 4). The OECD (2017b) reports that across countries that participate in PISA for financial literacy, "around 38% of the variation in financial literacy Financial Literacy Education in Ontario 313 scores reflects factors that are uniquely captured by the financial literacy assessment" (p. 68). The remaining variation is explained by differing results in math and reading. 

Financial literacy is correlated with positive financial behaviours such as having a bank account, planning for retirement, and lower levels of debt (OECD, 2017a). Students who scored well on financial literacy in the OECD PISA test, discussed further below, were more likely to say that they would save up for something they wanted but did not have the money for, rather than trying to borrow money from family or friends (OECD, 2017b). Financial literacy is thought to make it easier for individuals to navigate an increasingly complex financial marketplace, although this notion is contested by some legal scholars (Bramley, 2012;Willis, 2008). For example, financial literacy is thought to enable individuals to accurately assess and compare the cost of credit products and to avoid financial abuse (Expert Committee to Consider Financial Advisory and Financial Planning Policy Alternatives, 2016; OECD, 2017a). Governments also have asserted a connection between a financially literate population and stable financial markets and healthy national economy (Exec. Order No. 13646, 2013;OECD, 2016;Task Force on Financial Literacy, 2010;Williams, 2007). 

The perceived benefits of financial literacy have resulted in actions by Canadian governments, including federal and provincial financial literacy strategies, aimed at improving Canadians' levels of financial literacy (Autorité des Marchés Financiers, 2019; 

Financial Consumer Agency of Canada [FCAC], 2015a; Government of Ontario, 2019).

Canadian results from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) study of 15-year-olds found that although students' performance in math, reading, and science is associated with performance in financial literacy, "students who do well in the other domains will not necessarily do well in financial literacy: the financial literacy assessment also captures unique skills not measured in other domains" (CMEC, 2017, p. 4). The OECD (2017b) reports that across countries that participate in PISA for financial literacy, "around 38% of the variation in financial literacy Financial Literacy Education in Ontario 313 scores reflects factors that are uniquely captured by the financial literacy assessment" (p. 68). The remaining variation is explained by differing results in math and reading. 

Financial literacy is correlated with positive financial behaviours such as having a bank account, planning for retirement, and lower levels of debt (OECD, 2017a). Students who scored well on financial literacy in the OECD PISA test, discussed further below, were more likely to say that they would save up for something they wanted but did not have the money for, rather than trying to borrow money from family or friends (OECD, 2017b). Financial literacy is thought to make it easier for individuals to navigate an increasingly complex financial marketplace, although this notion is contested by some legal scholars (Bramley, 2012;Willis, 2008). For example, financial literacy is thought to enable individuals to accurately assess and compare the cost of credit products and to avoid financial abuse (Expert Committee to Consider Financial Advisory and Financial Planning Policy Alternatives, 2016; OECD, 2017a). Governments also have asserted a connection between a financially literate population and stable financial markets and healthy national economy (Exec. Order No. 13646, 2013;OECD, 2016;Task Force on Financial Literacy, 2010;Williams, 2007). 

The perceived benefits of financial literacy have resulted in actions by Canadian governments, including federal and provincial financial literacy strategies, aimed at improving Canadians' levels of financial literacy (Autorité des Marchés Financiers, 2019; 

Financial Consumer Agency of Canada [FCAC], 2015a; Government of Ontario, 2019).

documents.title: Assessing financial literacy among the young
documents.snippet: The inclusion of financial literacy into PISA has generated critical insights into the state of financial proficiency of the young around the globe. By benchmarking students' performance across countries, PISA enables policymakers, educators, and researchers to identify best practices, highlight areas for improvement, and develop evidence-based interventions to enhance adolescents' financial literacy levels. In this section, we report stylized results from the three waves in which the OECD administered the financial literacy questionnaires (2012, 2015 and 2018).

Until the last decade of the 20th century, comparisons of OECD learning outcomes were based mainly on the number of years of compulsory education, which was not a reliable criterion for assessing students' capabilities and competencies. In 2005, OECD first reviewed surveys in 12 of its member countries. Consequently, in October 2008, the OECD established a subgroup of financial literacy measurement to address the need for internationally comparable financial literacy and capability surveys (OECD, 2011), and this effort resulted in the establishment of the International Student Assessment Program (PISA). The goal of PISA was to directly test students' knowledge and skills through internationally agreed metrics. The additional socioeconomic background was to be obtained by linking data from students, teachers, and schools (Schleicher, 2018).

PISA also examined students' experiences and knowledge about money and provided an overall picture of the ability of 15-year-olds to apply their acquired knowledge and skills in real situations involving financial matters and decisions. In recent decades, many countries around the world became increasingly concerned about the level of financial literacy of their citizens, especially students and young people.

The PISA defines financial literacy as (OECD, 2014, p. 33):

"Knowledge and understanding of financial concepts and risks, and the skills, motivation, and confidence to apply such knowledge and understanding in order to make effective decisions across a range of financial contexts, to improve the financial well-being of individuals and society, and to enable participation in economic life."

The PISA study (OECD, 2017) took into account three different aspects of financial literacy:

• content: money and financial transactions, planning and management, risk and return, and financial environment;

• processes: identification of financial information, analysis of information in the financial context, evaluation of financial issues, understanding, and applying finance knowledge;

• contexts: education and work, household and family, personal finance, and company.

Prior to PISA financial literacy testing, little effort was made to collect data to compare the financial literacy of young people on a global scale. No systematic cross-country comparison or worldwide international research was conducted until 2012, but the PISA assessment has been carried out every three years since then. According to the financial literacy levels determined between one and five, 91% of the students were found to have a first-level or above financial literacy level. In comparison, 8% of the students had a fifth level of financial literacy. Türkiye and Romania did not participate in this financial literacy assessment. However, these two countries participated in the PISA assessments, including reading, mathematics, and science. While the OECD average financial literacy score was 498, two countries scored below this average. Eight countries scored above the OECD average (OECD, 2024). In this respect, determining the financial needs related to demand and providing well-planned financial education based on these determinations can increase individuals' financial satisfaction.
